silhouette

/SIL-oo-ET/ — stress on the last syllable, like ballet · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A silhouette is the dark outline or shape of a person or object seen against a lighter background.

At dusk, the lone oak stood as a black silhouette against the orange sky.

Worked Example

Against the sunset, a dancer's form stretched and bent as a dark, graceful silhouette.

Silhouette is precise because it captures not just any dark shape, but the specific dramatic effect of being backlit—a recognizable figure seen as a dark outline against bright light. The plain word "shape" wouldn't convey that visual drama.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

profile: A profile is the side view of a person's face — the single line of forehead, nose, and chin seen from the side. A silhouette is the whole dark form a person or object makes against a lighter background, from any angle. Profile names the viewpoint; silhouette names the lighting effect.

figure: A figure is the visible form of a person or body in any light — you can watch a figure stroll across a sunny street and still see its colors and details. A silhouette is a figure under one special condition: lit from behind, so it goes completely dark against the brightness.

cutout: A cutout is a flat shape scissored from paper or cardboard — a real object you could pick up and hold. A silhouette is not an object at all but an effect of light: the dark form something makes when strong light sits behind it. Old-fashioned silhouette portraits copied that dark form onto black paper.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

detail: a small, clearly visible individual feature

close-up: a near view revealing every fine feature

Where it sits · how sharply the dark figure stands out — shape → outline → shadow → silhouette

shape vs. silhouette: Shape is the loosest term compared with silhouette: a shape is any general form, while a silhouette is a specific dark form seen against a lighter background.

outline vs. silhouette: An outline is just the traced edge of something, while a silhouette fills that edge in with solid darkness set sharply against the light.

shadow vs. silhouette: A shadow is cast onto a surface by blocked light, but a silhouette is the dark figure itself, standing out crisply against a brighter background.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — Silhouette

Root — Silhouette: surname of Étienne de Silhouette, a French finance minister mocked for his cheap, bare-bones policies (French (eponym))

Put it together

Put it together: There are no word parts to assemble here: the whole word is the surname of Étienne de Silhouette, whose penny-pinching policies made his name a mocking label for the cheapest kind of portrait — a plain dark outline against a light background, with no costly detail.

Use the root in a new word: silhouetted

Use the root in a new word: silhouetted: When hikers stand silhouetted against the sunset, they appear as dark outlined shapes — the verb form of silhouette, the word born from a French minister's name.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral

Silhouette is perfect when you want to describe the dramatic visual effect of a dark form against a bright background. It's more specific than just "shape" or "outline" because it conveys the striking contrast and the figure's recognizability. Use it in art, photography, or vivid descriptions; "shape" works fine for everyday use.
